Electronic address: wmohr@mpi-bremen.de. * 3 Biogeochemistry Department, Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology, 28359 Bremen, Germany. * PMID: 28586682 * DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2017.03.030 Abstract Phytoplankton form the basis of the marine food web and are responsible for approximately half of global carbon dioxide (CO2) fixation (∼ 50 Pg of carbon per year). Thus, these microscopic, photosynthetic organisms are vital in controlling the atmospheric CO2 concentration and Earth's climate. Phytoplankton are dependent on sunlight and their CO2-fixation activity is therefore restricted to the upper, sunlit surface ocean (that is, the euphotic zone). CO2 usually does not limit phytoplankton growth due to its high concentration in seawater. However, the vast majority of oceanic surface waters are depleted in inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and/or silica; nutrients that limit primary production in the ocean (Figure 1). Phytoplankton growth is mainly supported by either the recycling of nutrients or by reintroduction of nutrients from deeper waters by mixing. A small percentage of primary production, though, is fueled by 'external' or 'new' nutrients and it is these nutrients that determine the amount of carbon that can be sequestered long term in the deep ocean. For most nutrients such as phosphorus, iron, and silica, the external supply is limited to atmospheric deposition and/or coastal and riverine inputs, whereas their main sink is the sedimentation of particulate matter. Nitrogen, however, has an additional, biological source, the fixation of N2 gas, as well as biological sinks via the processes of denitrification and anammox. Despite the comparatively small contributions to the overall turnover of nutrients in the ocean, it is these biological processes that determine the ocean's capacity to sequester CO2 from the atmosphere on time scales of ocean circulation (∼ 1000 years). This primer will highlight shifts in the traditional paradigms of nutrient limitation in the ocean, with a focus on the uniqueness of the nitrogen cycling and its biological sources and sinks. fetched_contents.text: Novel land-based tropical red macroalgae cultivation system is based on influent deep seawater as the nutrient and carbon sources Pilot land-based grow-out trials demonstrate the potential for large-scale production of Agardhiella subulata and Halymenia hawaiiana Macroalgae generate many valuable products with various applications such as food, nutraceuticals and pharmaceuticals as they contain various bioactive substances like polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and polyphenols with various properties including anticarcinogenic, antiviral, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anticoagulant activities. Seaweed farming is gaining attention as a source of climate, environmental and socioeconomic solutions, ranging from carbon dioxide mitigation and nutrient filtration to being a source of renewable feedstock materials for food, feed and biofuel. Assuming the long-term growth rate reported from 2000–2018 of 6.2 percent per year, global seaweed aquaculture is expected to reach production rates of 252 million metric tons (fresh weight) by 2050. Macroalgae aquaculture is an alternative to exploiting natural marine ecosystems for feedstuff. Land-based seaweed cultivation offers advantages in the production of high-value species over ocean-based farming with tighter control of biotic factors, including herbivory and disease, and abiotic factors, including optimized light, nutrient availability, seawater inputs and aeration. As biomass quality and productivity are highly dependent on the growing environment, seaweed farmers can reduce variability and obtain higher quantity and quality of targeted compounds in land-based systems, which is also important for product traceability and safety. In addition to variation in yields, the biochemical composition of the biomass can vary seasonally even in land-based culture systems but potentially less in tropical environments with lower seasonal climatic fluctuations. The seaweed compositional profile (i.e., the respective protein, carbohydrate and lipid content of the harvested biomass) is important to predict and plan the route the biomass can take for either conversion or toward applications in the aquaculture sector. The cultivation of macroalgae in tropical climates is primarily driven by the carrageenan industry (producing carrageenan, a complex sugar derived from red seaweeds), with the main focus on the red macroalgae Kappaphycus spp. and Eucheuma spp., while other species have been reported on with experimental trials only. Our study placed emphasis on two lesser-known species with promising commercial potential. This article – summarized from the original publication (Augyte, S. et al. 2023. Tropical Red Macroalgae Cultivation with a Focus on Compositional Analysis. Plants 2023, 12(20), 3524) – reports on a study to demonstrate the productivity of two commercially important tropical red macroalgae: Agardhiella subulata and Halymenia hawaiiana. Study setup For the onshore cultivation and growth experiments at Ocean Era, Inc., at the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority (NELHA) facility, outdoor tanks were set up directly connected to a seawater supply system. The 340-L capacity tanks were filled to 300 liters with flow rates at 50 turnovers per day. Three separate trials set up for the tropical red macroalgae A. subulata and H. hawaiiana at varying levels of deep-seawater (DSW) additions ranging from 0 to 10 percent to test the effects of nutrient additions on productivity. The seawater was continuously supplied from pipes connected to surface seawater (SSW) from the surface and deep seawater (DSW) pumped from pipes at 900 meters below the surface, with the nutrient composition of seawater continuously tested at the NELHA Water Quality Lab. The SSW is low in available nitrogen at 7.4 micrograms per liter (N/L), and the DSW has a high nutrient profile of 580.5 micrograms of nitrogen per liter, which could be supplemented to the tanks at various concentrations depending on experimental design. For these trials, a 10 percent addition of DSW was added with the combined nitrogen available at 64.7 micrograms N/L, a 5 percent addition of DSW at 36.1 micrograms N/L, a 1 percent addition of DSW at 13.1 micrograms N/L, and the 0 percent DSW contained 7.39 micrograms N/L. All tanks were aerated through a single diffuser hose running along the center of the length of the tank. A. subulata doubled its biomass when DSW additions were increased from 1 to 5 percent, while still maintaining its pigmentation, indicating it was no longer nitrogen-limited. We also confirmed that when the space limitation is removed and adequate nutrients are available, the macroalgae can reach growth rates of up to 26 percent. A rapid decrease in specific growth rates was observed as biomass increased in the tanks over time; therefore, developing a consistent harvesting strategy is recommended to avoid light, nutrient, and density limitations. fetched_contents.text: Physical processes that enhance nutrient transport and primary productivity in the coastal and open ocean of the subarctic NE Pacific Abstract In comparison to the open ocean, several additional processes including coastal upwelling, river discharge, tidal mixing, estuarine circulation and benthic remineralization enhance nutrient supply to the surface waters of the continental shelf. In general, coastal waters become nitrate-limited during the phytoplankton growing season, whereas iron and dissolved silicate limit phytoplankton growth in the less productive oceanic waters of the Gulf of Alaska. If coastal processes supply ample amounts of macro and micro nutrients during the growing season, diatom communities dominated by species such as Skeletomema costatum, Chaetoceros spp. and Thalassiosira spp. will bloom. Growth rates of these bloom populations typically range from 0.5 to >1.5 doublings per day, which place a high demand on nutrients. Any transport of coastal waters away from the shelf will enhance productivity in oceanic waters. The general circulation of the eastern subarctic Pacific does not allow for offshore transport except in special circumstances. These include anticyclonic mesoscale eddy formation, which can export as much as 5000 km3 of nutrient-rich waters from the shelf in a single eddy, and recirculation of waters away from southwestern Alaska due to the cyclonic circulation around the western edge of the Alaskan Gyre. Recirculation can carry nutrient-rich water from the coast to the vicinity of Ocean Station Papa (50°N, 145°W) within a few months. For both eddies and gyre recirculation, much of the water being carried into the open ocean lies below the euphotic zone. Iron enrichment occurs to a depth of at least 1000 m in the Gulf of Alaska as a result. Periods of enhanced eddy formation or recirculation may supply iron that enriches the open ocean for several years. Damming of the Columbia River and human uses of its waters have resulted in more winter and less summer discharge of fresh water and dissolved Si. Coastal currents in this area flow north in winter and south in summer. As a consequence, there has been a net temporal change in Si inputs to the ocean since the mid 1970s, with about 4×109 mol more Si flowing north in winter and 9×109 mol less Si flowing south in summer compared with the early 1900s. Since silicate limits diatom growth and diatoms are responsible for most carbon export in phytoplankton, implications for ocean productivity are significant. Introduction Coastal waters of the eastern subarctic Pacific are highly productive (Denman et al., 1981; Perry et al., 1989; Wheeler et al., 2003; Ianson et al., 2003; Stabeno et al., in press), supporting rich fisheries (Ware and McFarlane, 1989) that often fluctuate strongly over time as a result of climate variability (Hare and Francis, 1995; Beamish and Bouillon, 1993). The open ocean is also an important habitat for commercial fish species, and likewise experiences variable productivity that is commonly linked to mesoscale processes (Crawford et al., submitted), El Niño events (Whitney et al., 1998) and decadal oscillations (Brodeur and Ware, 1992). Some of the variability observed in both the shelf and oceanic region is due to the strength of water exchanges between these regions. An example of this include the northward advection of oceanic subtropical waters along the continental margin during strong Los Niños (Freeland, 2002), which results in the introduction of warmer, more saline, lower nutrient waters (Whitney and Welch, 2002), exotic zooplankton (Mackas and Galbraith, 2002) and fish (McFarlane and Beamish, 2001) along the coast of British Columbia. Major Los Niños also appear to influence the intensity of mesoscale eddy formation on the BC and Alaska coasts (Crawford, 2002), which then enhances the export of coastal waters and possibly juvenile fish (A. Sinclair, pers. comm.) into the deeper, oceanic region of the Gulf of Alaska. The Gulf of Alaska shelf is, in general, rich in iron (Chase et al., 2002; Johnson et al., submitted) and silicate (Whitney et al., in press), with the result that phytoplankton become nitrate-limited each summer (Whitney and Welch, 2002; Stabeno et al., in press; Childers and Whitledge, in press). On the other hand, phytoplankton growth in the high-nitrate, low-chlorophyll (HNLC) waters of the Alaskan Gyre is limited by iron (Martin and Fitzwater, 1988; Boyd et al., 1996; Nishioka et al., 2001) and occasionally silicate (Wong and Matear, 1999; Whitney et al., in press) but never by nitrate. Therefore, any exchange between these regions will mix waters replete in nitrate with those rich in iron. This certainly is the case with mesoscale eddies, which have been shown to transport substantial amounts of iron into HNLC waters (Johnson et al., submitted), thus increasing the productivity of oceanic waters (Peterson et al., submitted; Whitney and Robert, 2002). In this paper, we describe processes responsible for exporting nutrients and production from one region to another, and processes that increase the overall productivity of the Gulf of Alaska by injecting growth-limiting nutrients into surface waters. Experimental evidence supporting nutrient enrichment effects shows that nutrient addition can stimulate macroalgal biomass, growth, and physiological responses, but the strength of the effect depends on the design, species, and whether the system is limited by nutrients or other constraints.

Key experimental designs used to test nutrient addition effects include both laboratory and field experiments, with nutrient treatments applied either as pulses, continuous additions, or through seawater supply systems. One study explicitly describes nutrient enrichment experiments to assess the relationship between tissue nutrient concentration and macroalgal growth [N2-R1]. Another review notes that nutrient enrichment experiments have been used to test growth responses of macroalgae to ambient nutrient supply and experimental nutrient enrichment, using initial and final wet weights of Ulva spp. [N2-R2]. A broader study also reports that nutrient enrichment experiments were used to test whether adding nitrogen and phosphorus to an aquatic system stimulates multiple levels of food web responses [N2-R3]. This pattern indicates that experimental designs often measure biomass and growth directly, and sometimes track nutrient uptake or tissue composition [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

Measured responses such as biomass, growth rate, and element uptake are common outcomes. In one field study, macroalgal biomass and nutrient composition were measured to assess nutrient enrichment effects [N2-R5]. Another study reports that nutrient enrichment may significantly improve food quality by increasing biomass and altering nutrient content in macroalgae [N2-R5]. In the pilot deep-seawater cultivation study, biomass production was tracked over time, and nutrient additions had a significant effect on biomass, with A. subulata doubling biomass when DSW additions increased from 1 to 5 percent [N3-F2]. The same study also reports that nutrient addition improved productivity and that growth rates increased under sufficient nutrient conditions [N3-F2]. These results show that nutrient enrichment can increase biomass and, in some cases, improve biochemical composition or market value [N2-R5][N3-F2].

Evidence for nutrient limitation versus other growth constraints is mixed but strong in some cases. Nutrient limitation is a central theme in the literature: many nutrient-enrichment studies are designed to test whether ambient nutrient supply is insufficient to support growth [N2-R2][N2-R5]. In the deep-seawater cultivation system, the study explicitly states that low nutrient levels in tropical, oligotrophic coastal waters are a major constraint for macroalgae cultivation and that external inputs are usually required [N3-F2]. This suggests that the observed increases in biomass and productivity under enriched conditions are likely responses to nutrient limitation rather than to a generic growth boost [N3-F2]. The experimental evidence also supports the idea that nutrient addition can alleviate limitation, but not all species respond equally: one review notes that macroalgae species are differently affected by nutrient enrichment from aquaculture and agriculture [N3-R1]. This implies that nutrient limitation is context-dependent, and experimental designs must account for species-specific responses and environmental constraints [N3-R1][N3-F2].

Overall, the experimental evidence supports nutrient enrichment effects, but it also shows that the response depends on the experimental design, nutrient availability, and whether the system is nutrient-limited or constrained by other factors such as light, density, or space [N2-R2][N2-R5][N3-F2]. The evidence is strongest for biomass and growth responses, with some support for element uptake and compositional changes [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2].

Practical and ecological implications of using deep ocean water for macroalgal cultivation suggest that deep-sea water can be a feasible and scalable input for nutrient supply, but it carries ecological risks and is still largely in the pilot or experimental stage.

Feasibility and scalability depend on the ability to supply deep seawater consistently and efficiently. The cited pilot land-based system used deep seawater from 900 meters below the surface and added it to tanks at various concentrations (0–10 percent DSW) to test productivity [N3-F2]. The study found that nutrient additions significantly improved biomass production, with A. subulata doubling biomass when DSW additions increased from 1 to 5 percent and reaching up to 247.5 grams fresh weight per square meter per day under 10 percent DSW [N3-F2]. It also noted that growth rates can reach 26 percent under adequate nutrients, although they decline as biomass increases over time [N3-F2]. These results indicate that deep-seawater inputs can be used to improve productivity in controlled cultivation systems, especially in nutrient-depleted environments [N3-F2]. The study also highlights that land-based systems allow tighter control of biotic and abiotic factors, which can improve biomass quality and productivity [N3-F2]. This supports feasibility as a cultivation strategy, though scalability will depend on infrastructure, energy, and operational costs.

Current adoption or pilot program evidence shows that deep-sea water is already being tested in pilot systems, but commercialization remains limited. The cited source describes a novel land-based tropical red macroalgae cultivation system based on influent deep seawater as the nutrient and carbon source [N3-R3]. It reports pilot land-based grow-out trials demonstrating the potential for large-scale production of A. subulata and H. hawaiiana [N3-F2]. Another source notes that land-based seaweed cultivation is gaining attention as a source of climate, environmental, and socioeconomic solutions, with global seaweed aquaculture expected to reach 252 million metric tons fresh weight by 2050 [N3-F2]. While these statements are broader seaweed aquaculture claims, they contextualize the practical appeal of deep-seawater-based systems. The evidence is strongest for pilot-scale demonstration rather than widespread adoption [N3-F2][N3-R3].

Ecological risks and unintended consequences include potential nutrient cycling effects and ecosystem disruption. The cited deep-seawater study notes that the effects of deep-seawater pumping on global nutrient cycles would need to be evaluated [N5-R4]. A broader review on nutrient transport and productivity emphasizes that nutrient-rich deep waters do not disperse evenly at the ocean surface, which can create localized enrichment and uneven ecological impacts [N5-R3]. Another review states that artificial upwelling can supply nutrients for macroalgae farms, but the effects on global nutrient cycles need to be considered [N5-R4]. These points suggest that deep-sea water use could alter local nutrient dynamics, potentially favoring macroalgae at the expense of other species or creating unintended enrichment hotspots [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The cited pilot study also notes that increased biomass can create light, nutrient, and density limitations, implying that nutrient inputs may need to be carefully managed to avoid runaway growth or system instability [N3-F2].

In summary, deep-sea water appears feasible and scalable for macroalgal cultivation in controlled settings, with pilot evidence showing improved biomass and productivity [N3-F2][N3-R3]. However, the evidence also indicates ecological risks related to nutrient cycling and uneven dispersal, and the current adoption stage is more pilot-based than widespread commercial deployment [N5-R3][N5-R4][N3-F2].

The evidence suggests that deep waters are often richer in nutrients than surface waters because surface waters are frequently depleted in the major nutrients that limit marine productivity [N1-F1]. This means that deep-seawater inputs can help overcome nutrient limitation, which is a common constraint on macroalgal growth in nutrient-depleted environments [N1-F1][N3-F2].

The relevant evidence points to nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon as the central macronutrients that support macroalgal physiology [N1-R2]. The evidence suggests that deep waters are often richer in nutrients than surface waters because surface waters are frequently depleted in the major nutrients that limit marine productivity [N1-F1]. This means that deep-seawater inputs can help overcome nutrient limitation, which is a common constraint on macroalgal growth in nutrient-depleted environments [N1-F1][N3-F2].

The relevant evidence points to nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon as the central macronutrients that support macroalgal physiology [N1-R2]. In the context of deep ocean waters, the cited pilot system provides a concrete example: surface seawater had only 7.4 micrograms N/L, whereas deep seawater had 580.5 micrograms N/L, making deep water a valuable external nutrient source for cultivation [N3-F2]. ### 2) Ways deep ocean waters differ from surface waters in nutrient availability and stability

Deep ocean waters differ from surface waters in two key ways: **higher nutrient concentrations** and **greater stability**. The ocean-literature review states that most surface waters are depleted in inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus, iron, and/or silica, while nutrients are reintroduced from deeper waters by mixing [N1-F1]. The Southern Ocean review adds that deep waters can provide nutrient-rich inputs that increase productivity in surface waters [N5-F3]. The deep-seawater cultivation study further demonstrates that deep seawater can be used to supplement nutrient-depleted coastal waters, where external inputs are usually required for successful macroalgae cultivation [N3-F2].
